chapters.title: Chapter 2: Crude Oil and the Global Economy

lessons.title: How Crude Oil Prices Are Set: OPEC, Shale, and Geopolitics

children.text: Oil Doesn't Have One Price, It Has Three Benchmarks and a Risk Premium

When a news channel says 'oil is at $85', it is almost always quoting one specific benchmark, usually Brent, out of several that trade at meaningfully different prices at the same moment. Layered on top of whichever benchmark you look at are three forces that decide where it actually sits: how disciplined OPEC and its allies are being with supply, how quickly US shale producers respond to price signals, and how much of a geopolitical risk premium traders are willing to pay for insurance against a supply disruption that has not happened yet, and may never happen. This lesson takes each of these apart.

body.text: Crude oil's price is not one number. It is a benchmark, plus an OPEC+ discipline premium, plus a shale flexibility discount, plus whatever fear the market is currently pricing for a disruption that hasn't happened.

children.text: The Benchmarks You'll Actually See Quoted
As an Indian investor, the benchmark that matters most to you is not the one you'll see quoted on financial television by default.

cells: The global reference price for roughly two-thirds of internationally traded crude, and the one most commonly quoted in Indian financial media
The US domestic benchmark, priced and stored at Cushing, Oklahoma. Usually close to Brent but can diverge sharply, as it did in April 2020
The reference for most crude sold to Asia, including a large share of India's imports
A weighted average of Dubai and Brent grades
Published daily by the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC) under India's Ministry of Petroleum, this is the number that actually reflects what Indian refiners are paying

children.text: Since June 2017, Indian oil marketing companies revise retail petrol and diesel prices daily, tracking international benchmarks and the rupee's exchange rate rather than a fixed administered price. This means the Indian Crude Basket, not just the Brent headline number, is what ultimately feeds into what you pay at the pump.
OPEC+ and the Swing Producer System

markDefs.definition: Oil production capacity that a producer keeps deliberately idle, ready to bring online within a short period to offset a supply disruption elsewhere or to cool a price spike.

children.text: OPEC, the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries, and its wider OPEC+ grouping that includes Russia and other major producers, coordinate output quotas among member countries. Saudi Arabia, in particular, holds meaningful

, which lets it act as the closest thing the oil market has to a central bank: cutting output to defend a price floor when the market is oversupplied, or opening the taps to cool a price spike that risks demand destruction. This coordination is never perfect. Member countries routinely produce above their agreed quotas when prices are attractive, and compliance discipline is one of the most closely watched variables by anyone trading the oil cycle.
Shale: The Swing Producer That Doesn't Take Orders From Anyone

US shale producers do not coordinate output the way OPEC+ members do. Instead, thousands of individual companies respond to price signals directly: when prices rise well above breakeven, more wells get drilled within months, as covered in Chapter 1; when prices fall, drilling activity drops just as quickly. This is why the weekly US oil rig count, published by Baker Hughes, is one of the most widely tracked leading indicators in the entire industry. A falling rig count during a price slump signals that shale supply will shrink in the coming months, which is exactly the kind of signal that eventually helps a bust turn back into a recovery.

A large share of the world's traded crude has to physically pass through a small number of narrow shipping chokepoints, and the market prices in a permanent insurance premium against any of them being disrupted, even when nothing is currently wrong.

body.label: Strait of Hormuz
body.value: Roughly a fifth of global oil and gas liquids consumption
body.context: Widely cited estimates put around one-fifth of global oil and condensate consumption as transiting this single chokepoint between Iran and Oman. Any credible threat to it moves oil prices immediately, regardless of whether physical flows actually change.

body.title: Geopolitics and the Oil Price: A Quick History

events.title: The Arab Oil Embargo
events.description: OPEC members embargoed oil exports to countries supporting Israel in the Yom Kippur War, roughly quadrupling oil prices and introducing the world to the idea of oil as a geopolitical weapon.

events.title: The Iranian Revolution and Iran-Iraq War
events.description: Disruption to Iranian output, followed by war between Iran and Iraq, pushed prices to new highs and cemented the Middle East's central role in oil markets.

events.title: The Gulf War
events.description: Iraq's invasion of Kuwait removed a large chunk of global supply overnight, causing a sharp, if relatively short-lived, price spike.

events.title: The Shale Glut
events.description: Rapid growth in US shale output, combined with OPEC's decision not to cut production to defend price, drove crude from around $100 to near $30 a barrel.

events.title: The Covid Demand Collapse
events.description: Global lockdowns crushed oil demand almost overnight, and storage constraints briefly sent WTI futures negative, as covered in Chapter 1.

events.title: Russia's Invasion of Ukraine
events.description: Sanctions on Russian energy exports disrupted established trade flows, sent Brent above $120 a barrel, and led India to become one of the largest buyers of discounted Russian crude as global trade patterns reshuffled.

body.text: The 2022 shift mattered enormously for India specifically. As Western buyers stepped back from Russian crude under sanctions, Indian refiners bought it at a meaningful discount to Brent, which helped cushion India's import bill even as the headline benchmark price spiked. This is a good example of why the Indian Crude Basket can, at times, tell a different story from the Brent price alone.

body.title: Quick Check: Benchmark Recall
body.textWithBlank: The crude oil benchmark most commonly quoted in Indian financial media, extracted from fields in the North Sea, is called ___.
body.explanation: Brent is the reference price for roughly two-thirds of internationally traded crude oil and is the benchmark most often quoted in headlines, even though India's actual import cost tracks the Indian Crude Basket, a Dubai-Brent weighted average.

body.title: Show me: how the Indian Crude Basket is actually built

children.text: The Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell, a body under India's Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, publishes the Indian Crude Basket price daily. It is calculated as a weighted average of the Dubai and Oman grades and the Brent grade, weighted roughly in proportion to the actual mix of sour and sweet crude that Indian refiners process.

This number, not the Brent headline you see on a stock market ticker, is the one that historically drove government fuel subsidy calculations and continues to be the closest proxy for India's actual oil import cost. If you want to track India's real exposure to the oil cycle rather than the global headline, this is the series to follow.

points: Oil trades on several benchmarks at once. Brent is the global headline number, but the Indian Crude Basket, a Dubai-Brent weighted average, is what actually reflects India's import cost.

OPEC+ acts as a loose, imperfect central bank for oil supply, using spare capacity to manage price, while US shale responds to price signals directly and far faster, making the weekly rig count a useful leading indicator.

A permanent geopolitical risk premium sits on top of the fundamental price, driven by chokepoints like the Strait of Hormuz and by live conflicts and sanctions, and can move price sharply even without any actual change in physical supply.

2022's sanctions on Russian crude reshaped global trade flows and gave India access to discounted oil, a reminder that geopolitics can help as well as hurt a net oil importer, depending on which side of the disruption you sit on.
